A spatial receptor experiment gives you three kinds of data: gene expression
for each spot, receptor sequences, and the regions that you draw on the tissue.
These data must agree with each other. A receptor must belong to a spot that
exists. A clone column must exist in the receptor table. The SIRUP object keeps
all of the data in one place and checks these rules each time you change it.

This page explains the parts of the object, the rules that SIRUP checks, and the
functions that change the object. It has little code. For a hands-on start, read
`vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`.

The examples use a small synthetic object. It has 25 spots, 10 genes, 5 clones,
and 2 polygons. The spots and gene counts are simulated. The receptor rows are
real BCR sequences from a human thymus section, assigned to synthetic spots.

```{r load}
library(SIRUP)

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x
```

## The five parts

A SIRUP object is a list with five parts, in this order:

| Part | Contents | How to get it |
|---|---|---|
| `spatial` | The Seurat object, with expression and the H&E image | `getSpatial(x)` |
| `receptors` | The AIRR receptor table, as a tibble | `getReceptors(x)` |
| `metadata` | The field names and the image settings | `x$metadata` |
| `polygons` | The tissue regions, with one row for each polygon | `getPolygons(x)` |
| `analyses` | Results that you choose to keep | `getAnalysis(x, name)` |

The accessors return ordinary R objects. You can pass them to any function from
another package:

```{r parts}
getSpatial(x)
head(getReceptors(x), 3)
getPolygons(x)
```

`summary()` gives counts for each part:

```{r summary}
summary(x)
```

## Field names

Your receptor table can use any column names. SIRUP needs to know which column
plays which role. It stores this map in `x$metadata$receptor_fields`. There are
six fields:

| Field | The receptor column that holds... |
|---|---|
| `spatial_id` | the name of the spot that holds the receptor |
| `image` | the name of the Seurat image, if the object has several images |
| `sample` | the sample name, in a multi-sample object |
| `clone` | the clone ID |
| `locus` | the receptor locus, such as `IGH` or `TRB` |
| `count` | the number of reads or UMIs of the sequence |

```{r fields}
x$metadata$receptor_fields
```

You set the fields once, in `createSIRUP()`. After that, SIRUP functions find
each column without arguments. To change a field later, give a new map to
`updateReceptors()` with the `receptor_fields` argument. A value of `NULL` clears
an optional field.

## Rules that SIRUP checks

`validateSIRUP()` checks that the parts agree. It gives an error if one of these
rules fails:

1. The object has class `sirup`.
2. At least one receptor spatial ID matches a spot name in the Seurat object.
3. Each column that `receptor_fields` names exists in the receptor table.
4. If the `sample` field is set, the column exists in both the receptor table
   and the Seurat metadata.

```{r validate}
validateSIRUP(x, verbose = TRUE)
```

`createSIRUP()`, `updateReceptors()`, `updateSpatial()`, and the other functions
that change the object run this check before they return. A change that breaks
a rule fails at once and leaves your object as it was. This example gives every
receptor a spot name that does not exist:

```{r broken}
tryCatch(
  updateReceptors(x, function(receptors) {
    receptors$spatial_id <- "no-such-spot"
    receptors
  }),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  SIRUP keeps receptor rows that match no spot. Bulk and blood
  sequences are examples. The rules need only one match, so these rows stay in
  the table.
</div>

## Image settings

Two settings tell SIRUP how to put spots on the H&E image. Both live in
`x$metadata`:

* `image_scale` is the Seurat image scale, `"lowres"` or `"hires"`.
* `swap_coords` says whether to swap the x and y coordinates. Some older Seurat
  objects store the coordinates in the opposite order to the image.

Plots and spatial statistics read these settings when you leave their own
`image_scale` and `swap_coords` arguments at `NULL`. You set them once.

## Change the data

SIRUP does not wrap every AIRR tool. Three functions run any function on one
part of the object and put the result back:

* `updateReceptors(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getReceptors(x), ...)` and stores the
  table that `fun` returns.
* `updateSpatial(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getSpatial(x), ...)` and stores the
  Seurat object that `fun` returns.
* `updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ...)` does the same for a stored analysis.

Each function validates the object again before it returns. This call removes
the sequences of one clone:

```{r update-receptors}
x2 <- updateReceptors(x, dplyr::filter, clone_id != "3")
c(before = nrow(getReceptors(x)), after = nrow(getReceptors(x2)))
```

This call adds a column to the Seurat metadata:

```{r update-spatial}
x3 <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  spatial$gene_rich <- spatial$nFeature_Spatial >= 8
  spatial
})
table(getSpatial(x3)$gene_rich)
```

The same pattern runs germline reconstruction (`dowser::createGermlines()`) or
mutation counting (`shazam::observedMutations()`) inside the object.
`vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP")` shows these steps.

## Regions in the object

A region is a polygon on the tissue image. `addPolygons()` stores the polygons
and then marks the polygon of each spot and each receptor. It adds a
`polygon_id` column and one logical `polygon_<ID>` column for each polygon to
both the Seurat metadata and the receptor table:

```{r polygon-columns}
grep("^polygon", names(getReceptors(x)), value = TRUE)
grep("^polygon", names(getSpatial(x)[[]]), value = TRUE)
```

A spot on the edge of a polygon counts as a member when `include_boundary` is
`TRUE`, which is the default. `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")` shows how
to draw regions and measure what they hold.

## Several samples

`createSIRUP()` accepts one Seurat object or a named list of Seurat objects. With
a list, the `sample` column of the receptor table names the list entry of each
row. Rows with no matching entry stay in the table as non-spatial records. Bulk
and blood sequences use this feature. `mergeSIRUP()` joins several objects into one. `subsetSIRUP()` keeps chosen
samples, spots, or receptor rows. `getSpatial()` and `getReceptors()` return the
data of one sample when you give `sample`.
`vignette("multisample", package = "SIRUP")` has a full example.

## Keep results with the data

`setAnalysis()` stores any R object under a name. Use it for clones, trees,
spatial statistics, and polygon summaries. Stored results stay with the data
that made them, so you do not track separate files:

```{r analyses}
x <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5)
listAnalyses(x)
getAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
x <- removeAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
listAnalyses(x)
```

`saveSIRUP()` validates the object and writes it to one RDS file. The file also
records the versions of SIRUP and SeuratObject that wrote it. `readSIRUP()` reads
the file and does four things. It converts an object saved under the old package
name (SIRAP). It upgrades an older object to the current layout. It warns you if
the package versions differ from the file. It validates the object.

```{r save-read}
path <- saveSIRUP(x, tempfile(fileext = ".sirup.rds"))
x_again <- readSIRUP(path)
x_again
```
